Question Choices: Enter the lower and upper bounds of the principal range of arcsin(x). Angles are in radians.
Hints: Sine is restricted to a one-to-one interval.|Use Quadrants IV and I including endpoints.
Solution: The principal arcsine returns the unique angle in [-pi/2,pi/2] whose sine equals the input. Its input domain is [-1,1], and both range endpoints are included. The principal range is [-pi/2,pi/2].

Question Choices: Enter the lower and upper bounds of the principal range of arccos(x). Angles are in radians.
Hints: Cosine is restricted from 0 through pi.|The interval includes both endpoints.
Solution: The principal arccosine returns the unique angle in [0,pi] whose cosine equals the input. Its input domain is [-1,1], and both range endpoints are included. The principal range is [0,pi].

Question Choices: Enter the lower and upper bounds approached by the range of arctan(x). Angles are in radians.
Hints: Arctangent outputs angles between its horizontal asymptotes.|The endpoints are not included.
Solution: The principal arctangent returns the unique angle in (-pi/2,pi/2) whose tangent equals the input. Every real input is allowed; the range endpoints are excluded. The range lies between -pi/2 and pi/2.

Question Choices: Find arcsin(1). Angles are in radians.
Hints: Choose the principal angle whose sine is 1.|The top of the unit circle has angle pi/2.
Solution: The principal arcsine returns the unique angle in [-pi/2,pi/2] whose sine equals the input. Its input domain is [-1,1], and both range endpoints are included. arcsin(1)=pi/2.

Question Choices: Find arccos(-1). Angles are in radians.
Hints: Choose the principal angle whose cosine is -1.|The leftmost unit-circle point has angle pi.
Solution: The principal arccosine returns the unique angle in [0,pi] whose cosine equals the input. Its input domain is [-1,1], and both range endpoints are included. arccos(-1)=pi.

Question Choices: Find arctan(1). Angles are in radians.
Hints: Choose the principal angle with equal sine and cosine.|tan(pi/4)=1.
Solution: The principal arctangent returns the unique angle in (-pi/2,pi/2) whose tangent equals the input. Every real input is allowed; the range endpoints are excluded. arctan(1)=pi/4.

Question Choices: Find arcsin(sin(3pi/4)). Angles are in radians.
Hints: The output must lie in the arcsine principal range.|Find the principal angle with the same sine value.
Solution: Evaluate the inner sine, then choose the angle with that sine inside [-pi/2,pi/2]. Arcsine need not return the original angle if it is outside this principal interval. sin(3pi/4)=sqrt2/2 so arcsin returns pi/4.

Solution: Arctan maps every real input into (-pi/2,pi/2), where tangent is defined and one-to-one. Applying tangent recovers that input. tan(arctan(5))=5.

Question Choices: Why must a trigonometric function's domain be restricted before defining its inverse?
Question Answers: to make it one-to-one|it must be one-to-one|to pass the horizontal line test
Hints: Periodic functions repeat outputs.|An inverse function requires unique inputs for outputs.
Solution: An inverse on the original function's range is a function exactly when the original is one-to-one: distinct inputs give distinct outputs. A horizontal line may meet its graph at most once. A parabola on all reals fails, but its right branch is one-to-one. The domain is restricted so the trig function is one-to-one.

Question Choices: A ramp rises 3 units over a horizontal run of 4 units. Find its angle of elevation to the nearest tenth of a degree.
Solution: The rise is opposite and the horizontal run is adjacent, so tan(theta)=rise/run. Use arctan in degree mode and round only the final result. theta=arctan(0.75) is about 36.9 degrees.
